newsitem.title: GREECE: Albanian PM Fino secures support from EU, OSCE.
newsitem.headline: Albanian PM Fino secures support from EU, OSCE.

text.p: Visiting Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino secured much-needed support for his chaotic Balkan country on Thursday from the European Union and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).

EU, OSCE and Greek officials assured the 34-year-old Fino that his all-party unity government would get economic, organisational and humanitarian aid, as well as the peacekeepers needed to distribute it.

"The message from the talks is that the Albanian people have the support of the international community for the restoration of normalcy in Albania, free elections in June and economic development," Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos said.

He was speaking to reporters after a meeting with Fino, special OSCE envoy for Albania Franz Vranitzky, the former Austrian chancellor, and Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, current president of the EU general affairs council.
The EU and OSCE envoys rushed to Athens to meet Fino, who arrived on Wednesday for an official visit, and was feted with a military band at the airport and a posh state dinner under the Acropolis.

Analysts said the red-carpet treatment and the initiative taken by the two Western envoys to meet him in Athens was meant as a boost to Fino's unity government, which must cope with a deep economic crisis and lawlessness, and prepare a national election in June.
"The EU and OSCE reconfirmed their support for the coalition government," Fino told reporters. "The elections in June will be free and democratic, closely watched by the EU and OSCE."

Apart from an $80 million favourable loan from Greece, Fino secured logistical help to reconstruct Albania's shattered army, OSCE's presence to secure fair elections and a U.N.-approved force to make it all possible.
The Italian-led, multinational force of about 5,000 men will try to secure the ports of Durres and Vlore and Tirana airport for the delivery of aid to the impoverished country.
So far Italy is expected to provide 2,000 to 2,500 troops, France 1,000, Greece 700, Turkey 500, Spain 500 and Romania 400.
Pangalos said Albania preferred the force to be composed of mixed units and not divided into national contingents and that Greece agreed with the idea.

Anti-Italian public sentiment in Albania after the sinking of a boat packed with Albanian refugees in the Adriatic last week should not pose problems for the deployment of the force, he said. More than 80 people are feared dead in the incident.
"I believe the peace force deployment will go smoothly and will enjoy public support," he told a news conference after the meeting. "The (incident) was most probably an accident."
Rome has said the force could be deployed by about April 12.
"The main point is economic and humanitarian aid and, in order to make it work, we need the multinational force to protect it," Vranitsky said.
Asked if the April 12 deadline was realistic, he said: "Meeting this deadline is a bit over-optimistic but things won't change if we have plus or minus five days."

A revolt prompted by the collapse of popular pyramid savings schemes which left thousands destitute has left southern Albania lawless for weeks, with groups armed with weapons looted from army depots roaming the area.

Rebel committees in the south say they are trying to stop the violence that has killed scores of people but insist on the resignation of President Sali Berisha, blaming him for the collapse of the investment schemes.
Berisha has refused to resign but was forced to appoint the socialist Fino to head a 10-party government until the election.

Athens is deeply concerned about the crisis at its northern border, both for the effect of last month's insurrection on the large Greek minority living in the south and for a new wave of illegal Albanian immigrants from the former communist state.
Hundreds of thousands of illegal foreign workers, mostly the result of an Albanian refugee influx after the fall of communism in 1990, are already taxing the fragile Greek economy.
